title: Rewiring the State — Eoin Mulgrew, No. 10 (Downing Street)

primary.label: AI Platforms & Developer Tooling
primary.rationale: 10 DS functions as a central developer platform team building reusable AI tools and infrastructure that other government departments build on. The talk focuses on internal government workflows, operations, and knowledge work across UK public sector departments. Deployed tools are in daily use, scaling ambitions target horizontal use cases across the civil service, and AI tutors are evaluated against safety benchmarks. The talk is accessible to a general audience but references organizational and technical concepts that benefit from AI engineering context. This is a conference presentation with live demos, slides, and a Q&A session. Claims are stated directly in the transcript with quantitative supporting figures.

summary: Eoin Mulgrew introduces himself as running cross-government transformation work at the Number 10 data science team (10 DS), a unit established during the pandemic to ensure the most important national decisions are informed by the best evidence. The team is now scaling AI engineering capability across strategically important parts of the state. He frames the context: the UK faces severe public service delivery challenges including 7.25 million people on NHS waiting lists, 350,000 court cases in backlog, and only one in five planning decisions made on time, underpinned by a public sector productivity crisis estimated at £40 billion in potential annual AI-driven gains. Government, an industry of 400,000 people—most of whom are call center operators, prison wardens, and nurses—has historically struggled to build high-performing technical teams due to pay gaps, hierarchy, bureaucracy, and necessary safeguards. The response is a novel "insurgency model": a small unit at the center with a Number 10 mandate, unusually high political backing, market-rate pay, high autonomy, and a grueling 0.7–0.8% acceptance rate recruiting exclusively from outside the civil service. Mulgrew emphasizes recruiting missionaries, not mercenaries. The team operates in two modes: tackling low-hanging fruit themselves via forward-deployed engineers embedding with policy, legal, comms, and operational teams, and partnering on complex systemic problems. Demos include a policy simulation tool, a statute book analysis tool that replaced a £1.5M external legal contract, a delivery red-teaming PMO that flags optimism bias and risk-rating patterns to Number 10 decision makers, and two public-facing dashboards—unprecedented in government—including one tracking the AI Opportunities Action Plan. A new public service went from idea to live in two months. Beyond the building, 10 DS partners with three teams: the AI Safety Institute, the Incubator for AI (building Extract with DeepMind/Gemini, digitizing handwritten planning applications rolling out nationally), and Just AI (MOJ team embedding engineers in prisons). Education work evaluates AI tutor models against safety and cognitive-load benchmarks. Mulgrew closes with a photo of Will, a Harvard dropout and YC founder, outside HMP Wandsworth with prison keys in his second week—embodying the pitch: come join us and we'll give you the keys to the state. The Q&A addresses model sycophancy (mitigated via red-teaming and user upskilling), scaling (horizontal use cases applied en masse across the system), AI tutors in education (government plans to set benchmarks and guardrails rather than compete with EdTech products, with initial testing involving 70 teachers role-playing as pupils; student motivation remains unaddressed), and international collaboration (some contact with US government initiatives and Singapore, but could do more; open to Norwegian contacts).
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: Introduction and Context
sections.summary: Mulgrew introduces himself and the 10 DS team, set up during the pandemic to ensure national decisions are informed by best evidence. He frames UK public service delivery challenges and the productivity crisis as the backdrop for radical AI adoption.

sections.title: Why Government Struggles with Technical Teams
sections.summary: Outlines traditional barriers: pay gaps, hierarchy, bureaucracy, slow movement, and necessary regulatory safeguards that make government unappealing to high-performing technical talent. Systemic change is beyond any single team.

sections.title: The Insurgency Model
sections.summary: Describes the novel operating model: a small unit with Number 10 mandate, high political backing, market-rate pay within reason, high autonomy, and exclusive external recruitment with a 0.7–0.8% acceptance rate. Emphasizes recruiting missionaries, not mercenaries, and cautions that political mandate alone is insufficient.

sections.title: Operating Modes and First Demos
sections.summary: Explains two operating modes: low-hanging fruit handled in-house by forward-deployed engineers, and complex problems handled via partnerships. Shows a policy simulation tool and the statute book analysis tool that saved £1.5M and delivered reusable capability. Begins describing the delivery red-teaming PMO.

sections.title: Delivery Red-Teaming PMO and Public Dashboards
sections.summary: Details the delivery red-teaming PMO tool that flags optimism bias and risk-rating patterns to Number 10 decision makers, now used daily. Notes two public-facing dashboards published within two months—unprecedented in UK government—including the AI Opportunities Action Plan tracker. Mentions an upcoming public service launch going from idea to live in two months.

sections.title: Ecosystem Partnerships: AISI, Incubator for AI, and Just AI
sections.summary: Covers three partner teams. AISI is the world's first government body for evaluating frontier models, supported by 10 DS fellows including Dr. Harry Coppock who led the Inspect tool. The Incubator for AI, a spin-out in DSIT, built Extract with DeepMind/Gemini to digitize handwritten planning applications, now rolling out nationally. Just AI, founded by former fellow Dan James in MOJ, embeds engineers in prisons for drug interdiction and security. Education work evaluates AI tutor models against safety and cognitive-load benchmarks.

sections.title: Closing: Will's Story and Recruitment Pitch
sections.summary: Closes with a photo of Will, a Harvard dropout and YC founder, outside HMP Wandsworth with prison keys in his second week—embodying the pitch to give talented outsiders the keys to the state. Summarizes proof points: saving money, shipping services at unprecedented speed, reforming frontline services. Ends as a recruitment pitch.

sections.title: Q&A: Sycophancy and Scaling
sections.summary: Addresses model sycophancy risk in policy tools, mitigated through pre-deployment red-teaming and user upskilling. On scaling, acknowledges the oil tanker metaphor, the need for strategic intervention to make the insurgency model the norm, and plans for horizontal process-level work across the 400,000-person civil service.

sections.title: Q&A: AI Tutors, Education Approach, and International Collaboration
sections.summary: Continues scaling answer, expressing ambition to pursue horizontal use cases applicable en masse across the system. An EdTech audience member asks about AI tutors in schools and student motivation; Mulgrew clarifies government plans to set benchmarks and guardrails for school adoption rather than competing with commercial products, notes initial testing with 70 teachers role-playing as pupils, and admits student uptake is not yet addressed. A Norwegian attendee asks about international collaboration; Mulgrew notes some contact with US government initiatives (task force, US Digital Service) and Singapore, but acknowledges they could do more and welcomes Norwegian contacts. Talk ends with applause.
